subtopics.title: The Table's Architecture — Atomic Number, Groups and Periods

questions.question: The modern periodic table arranges the elements in order of increasing:
The period number of an element equals its number of:
Elements in the same group behave similarly because they have the same number of:
options: Valence electrons — electrons in the outermost level

questions.question: An element with configuration 1s two, 2s two, 2p six, 3s two, 3p five sits in:
options: Period 3, group 17 — three occupied levels, seven valence electrons: chlorine

questions.question: Relative to the staircase line, the three kingdoms sit:
options: Metals upper right; non-metals left; metalloids at the bottom
Metals to the left; non-metals to the upper right; metalloids along the staircase
Non-metals to the left; metals upper right; metalloids in group 18

questions.question: Metals conduct electricity well because:
options: Their structure holds a sea of mobile electrons

questions.question: The ion habits of the two sides of the staircase are:
options: Metals lose electrons to form cations; non-metals gain electrons to form anions
Metals gain electrons; non-metals lose them

questions.question: Silicon is essential to electronics because, as a metalloid, it is:
options: A semiconductor — conducting between metal and insulator, and controllably so

subtopics.title: Trends Across and Down — Radius, Ionisation Energy, Electronegativity

questions.question: Across a period from left to right, atomic radius:
options: Decreases — more protons pull on the same outer level, reeling it inward

questions.question: Ionisation energy is the energy needed to:
options: Add an electron to an atom
Remove an electron from an atom — it rises across a period and falls down a group

questions.question: Down a group, ionisation energy decreases because the outer electron is:
options: Further from the nucleus and screened by more inner levels

questions.question: The most electronegative element, at the table's top right, is:
options: Fluorine — the noble gases sit out the trend because they rarely bond

subtopics.title: Group Portraits — Alkali Metals to Noble Gases

questions.question: Group 1 metals are the most reactive metals because they:
options: Have one cheap-to-lose valence electron, forming plus-one ions

questions.question: Going down group 1, reactivity:
options: Increases — the outer electron sits further out, more screened, and leaves more easily

questions.question: Going down group 17, reactivity:
options: Decreases — fluorine grips new electrons ferociously, iodine only mildly

questions.question: The noble gases of group 18 are unreactive because they:
options: Have full outer levels — nothing to lose, nothing to gain

subtopics.title: The Street Map of the Elements

questions.question: In the street-map picture, the row you live in tells you:
options: How many floors of electrons your house has

questions.question: Everyone in the same column shares the same:
options: Number of top-floor (valence) electrons — which sets their chemical family

questions.question: An element whose configuration ends at 2s two lives at the address:
options: Row 2, column 2 — two floors, two upstairs: beryllium

questions.question: Walking across a row, the atoms get smaller because each step adds:
options: A proton to the pulling team while the rope length stays the same

questions.question: Walking down a column, the nucleus's grip on the outer electrons weakens because:
options: The rope gets longer — a new level each row — and inner floors muffle the pull

questions.question: Fluorine is the fiercest electron-puller on the table because it combines:
options: A long rope with few pullers
A short rope with a big pulling team — top right of the table
The most neutrons with the fewest protons
A full outer level with no charge

questions.question: Potassium reacts more wildly with water than sodium because its one coin — its valence electron — is:
options: A floor higher, on a longer rope with a weaker grip, so it drops even more easily

questions.question: The mirror rule for reactivity going down the table is:
options: Both givers and collectors strengthen downward
Reactivity never changes within a family
Givers (metals) strengthen downward; collectors (halogens) weaken downward

questions.question: Balloons and old shop signs are filled with noble gases because these gases:
options: Glow on their own in daylight
React with essentially nothing — their outer levels are already full
